utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Matthew Olmsted, and Crispian Smith case manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Igor Pantelic appealing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I deal before we move to cross-examination of the witness with some of the matters both arising out of yesterday and the meeting that we had this morning. Your Honours invited us, the Defence and the Prosecution, to meet to discuss the question in particular of the 92 bis witnesses, and we had the meeting this morning, and, Your Honours, effectively, can I say this: The two sides are, in fact, at idem on this as aspect, to the extent. The Defence are entitled under the Rule to have the Prosecution submit its passages, that is to say such statements or transcripts as it relies on and such documents. In which event -- and then to either indicate that they agree them or do not agree them. And can I emphasise this: It is still within the Chamber's discretion as to whether to have the witnesses called for cross-examination. So, Your Honours, in fact, yesterday's discussion really is moot. We have to complete disclosure for all the witnesses because of the six-week rule that Your Honours imposed -- or time gap, I should say, between the -- yes. I don't think we're going to need the witness for the next 15 minutes. Thank you. Because of the time gap between the disclosure being completed and the witness being called. We are going to complete disclosure. Then we are going to file the packages and then we will see where we are. Your Honours, can I say this, however: The Defence have made the concession that for the -- the 92 -- the proposed 92 bis witnesses they will not ask for the full six weeks but will content with a four weeks' gap before the witnesses are called, if they are called. Can I just urge Your Honours to -- if I can put it this way, reconsider the decision that 92 ter is not to be used for this reason: If the Defence require the witnesses to be called for cross-examination and if Your Honours accede to that and on Your Honours' present ruling the witness will be completely viva voce, then, for example, can I give you one example for one witness for one adjudicated fact, and I'm giving that example simply because I happened to be looking at the witness yesterday for timing. The adjudicated fact is fact 193, and 193 deals with the circumstances of life in Banja Luka. That was in whole rejected under the head of "Unclear or misleading" in the context. The two witnesses, Your Honours, selected for that, if called viva voce, will be going through in each case not less than three hours' testimony, because it covers just about everything they say. It's not just a small adjudicated fact. Can I return to Manjaca, was it a detention camp. It is a huge adjudicated fact which deals with conditions of life in Banja Luka. That witness will then have to be called if the Defence said we want to cross-examine and Your Honours acceded to it, be called viva voce. It's not a simple fact. It would take no less than three hours to cover everything. In addition, Your Honours, the witnesses will have the added problem of dealing with events now some 19 -- not quite -- 18 years ago. So, Your Honours, I simply flag that out but for the simple problem or the simple answer to that is we will complete disclosure and then we'll file the 92 bis packages in the normal way. But, Your Honours, I would urge Your Honours to have a look at 92 bis (C). Your Honours, that's the first matter. The second matter is this: The law library, can I tell Your Honours, is effectively agreed. We're just waiting for one more document but we'll file this week, we've finally reached agreement on what goes into it. Third matter is exhumations. Your Honours, we have not been able to reach agree on this at all. In particular, the issue is whether we should be allowed to put into evidence, however it's done, by database or by a witness, evidence which relates to victims of the activities that are covered by this indictment who are not named in the schedules, and can I put it this way: Since the schedules were originally drafted as Your Honours may not be aware, more and more evidence comes in, and indeed the schedules specifically say this is not all of the victims in the particular area. We need to argue that before Your Honours before we really go any further, because a number of the matters hinge on what we are allowed to put into evidence. So, Your Honours, can we just for these purposes indicate Your Honours need to set aside a period of time when we can have full oral argument on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Korner. Could I just ask for clarification, whether your intervention is to be understood so as to mean that the -- that no agreement is or can be reached to hear any of the 19 witnesses or to have the evidence of any of the 19 witness -- or 29 witnesses I think it is, 29 witnesses as under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honours. What the Defence are saying, as Mr. Zecevic said yesterday, is they will not given us an indication as Your Honours invited us to do now. They will wait for us to file in the normal way the packages for those 29 witnesses, and then they will respond as to whether they accept it or they invite Your Honours, in Your Honours' discretion, I underline and emphasise that, to have the witness called. Now, that's where the -- the timing problem, if you like, arises, that Your Honours' present view is that no 92 ter, whereas 92 bis (C) effectively says the witness will be called, the package will be go in but the Defence will cross-examine. That's it. So there is no examination-in-chief because what they said before goes in or such parts that are obviously indicated as relevant. But Your Honours are saying we have to call them viva voce. Now, that as I say, and I merely picked a particular witness, to show that will undoubtedly, if Your Honours do not -- if Your Honours accede to the Defence request to have the witnesses called for -- called, then we are really stretching this case out quite a long way if we have to call these witnesses viva voce, many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As I understand the problem, Mrs. Korner, it is the following: If we accept a 92 ter package --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Bis. No if we accept a package that -- as you want to do it under 92 ter --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- then there would be no way for the Chamber to disallow the Defence to put questions to every single bit of that total package. So the idea of giving preference to viva voce was simply to allow the Chamber to control more efficiently the scope of the testimony of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, because what -- we've partly discussed this yesterday. We are obliged to highlight the particular part of the statement or transcript that goes to the 92 ter and also the context. We said we've got to have some sort of context. So I say this, I hope nobody's going to be sending e-mails saying you shouldn't be saying this, what our proposal is that we will highlight the part that relates to the adjudicated fact in one colour and then the part of the statement or transcript which we say is vital. So the context of the adjudicated fact in another. Now, the cross-examination is a different matter. We've slightly touched on this, Your Honours. How -- how you propose to limit cross-examination is another matter. Your Honours can limit it, I suppose, to this extent, that it can be factually limited to the adjudicated fact, but of course where credibility is concerned, that's another matter. The Defence have a right to cross-examine in relation to credibility, but that's the same either way, Your Honours. I mean, whether -- whether it's 92 ter or viva voce. That's why I'm slightly concerned about Your Honours -- so, 21, Your Honours. I'm reminded. Thank you for interrupting my train of thought, Mr. Olmsted. It's 21 witnesses, it's not 29. Either way, whether they're call viva or whether they are 92 ter, the cross-examination problem is the same, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Not -- not entirely. Not unless -- not unless we can force the Defence, and there is no way we can force the Defence under the rules, to limit its cross-examination to the adjudicated fact. The Defence is fully entitled to put questions to every bit and piece of the documents that -- that are presented under the 92 ter package and there is no way in the world that we can prevent the Defence from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: They're fully entitled to it and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour -- viva voce is the same. But that's it, Your Honours. I mean, viva voce or whatever, it's the same, because they'll have the statements and if they want to explore -- Your Honours, if we say the 92 ter package, the only part that is admitted is the adjudicated fact plus that part of the context that we say is so Your Honours can understand it, well, then the Defence -- if Your Honours take that view and I'm not sure that's right, I think Your Honours do have a certain part, a limit cross-examination to that part which is admitted and matters that relate to credibility, but we're slightly drifting off -- Your Honours, that may be another matter. As I say, the instant matter is what's going to happen now and that's what is going to happen now as I just explained. We'll file the packages and then it's a matter for the Defence and Your Honours to decide whether these witnesses can be 92 bis. And as I say, Your Honours will have to consider even if the Defence do object whether that's right. Your Honours, the -- I've dealt with the exhumation aspect. Your Honour, just -- I'm just checking that -- if there was -- no, apart from that, but, Your Honours, can I quickly go back over yesterday's 92 ter objection by Mr. O'Sullivan, because Your Honours have said you haven't ruled yet entirely on it. Your Honours, I'm sorry to see this was happening yet again exactly virtually the same thing that happened in respect of Mr. Treanor by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you here, Ms. Korner. We appreciate that yesterday's ruling on the -- I was going to say formal, but that's not correct, on the application, and having regard to what Mr. O'Sullivan said has created it's own set of problems, and as we indicated when we came back into court following the first break yesterday, it's a matter we have under active consideration. So I think I appreciate everything you're about to say, and we are alive to those problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And it's something with which we have to deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honours, I know that something was said about this yesterday by Mr. Hannis about this, but -- but really, it is not right for Mr. O'Sullivan at the end to stand up and object without having made his objection clear in advance and he cannot say he wasn't aware of this, because I said this in terms the last time he did it, that he has an obligation to inform us and the Trial Chamber in advance when there is an objection. His argument at the end that we should have guessed that this was going to happen is simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You need not argue this point, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Then, Your Honours, I'm -- because I was going to invite Your Honours to look at one of the articles, in particular to show why no doubt Your Honours admitted it and how important it is, but I'll deal with that if I'm allowed on later occasion. Your Honours, finally though, however, can I ask we need a decision on Witness ST-23, whether he's 92 ter or not. Can I go into private -- could we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt the discussion which I regret to say I can hear parts of, but can I just say I have been sent an e-mail by Ms. Pidwell that there may be time next Friday, the 27th of August, to argue the exhumations matter because we may have witness problems then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, madam. Before I invite counsel to begin his cross-examination, I would remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will try to proceed in the same manner that the Prosecutor used during his examination-in-chief and follow the same order, and I will just try to fill the blanks that, according to the Defence, appeared in your evidence during examination-in-chief. Could you just briefly confirm, please, that for a while you were employed as a secretary in the government of the -- of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you were employed in the -- at the highest level of the state administration or government, and could you now please just confirm for us that the Ministry of the Interior, and in future we shall refer to it as the police, was part of government or the state administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The work and structure of this agency and the proceedings that were carried out were subject to the legal -- to the laws on state administration, the law on administration, the law on proceedings and procedure, et cetera, and many other laws.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were applicable both in the work of the Ministry of the Interior and in the actions that they took.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, the Ministry of the Interior, or the police, was a specific government body, because, among other matters, it was authorised to deal with detection of crimes, identifying as perpetrators, detention of those perpetrators, and their hand-over to the competent judicial authorities for further legal processing; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I stressed this yesterday. At the time in question, they were referred to as organs of the interior. Today we call them the police. The work and the procedure applied within the organ of the interior at the time was regulated or followed the administrative procedure up until the moment when a criminal complaint was issued. The criminal complaint was subject to the law on criminal procedure, and it followed the rules thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Therefore, before they submit a criminal complaint or a criminal report, the police was duty-bound, among other matters, to secure and preserve material trace evidence of a crime, and it could attach to the criminal report also a preliminary interview with the suspects and witnesses, and all of this material would then be attached to the criminal report as submitted to the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The preliminary interviews, both of suspects and witnesses, followed -- they conducted according to the procedure that was regulated within the police. However, the searches and investigations were something that fell under the jurisdiction of the law on criminal procedure and the rules thereof had to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If a prosecutor who has received a criminal complaint and accompanying documents concludes this, that there is no sufficient -- that there are not enough documents that would justify a criminal -- further criminal procedure, then they could return it to the police and instruct the police that they should take certain actions and complete the materials within those bounds.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At that phase the prosecutor would issue instructions to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, let us deal with this issue in -- in more detail. This procedure, up until the prosecutor receives the complaint, was not considered a criminal proceeding. In the law there was a term used which was "preliminary procedures."

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's the term that I used yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In other words, all of the materials that were collected in that -- at that stage were not considered evidence which was sufficient to issue an indictment, nor could an indictment be based on those actions that the police had taken so far and the information that was collected so far by the police.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please just -- there should be an intervention in the transcript. It's not -- I did not say an indictment, I said "judgement." What would I like to explore with you is the preliminary interview that we also mentioned yesterday. You will agree with me that the Trial Chamber, which was to judge and lead the proceedings, were not allowed to see those preliminary interviews, nor could they -- nor could they found their decision on that basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the investigating judge conducts an investigation and after it has done so, it is his responsibility to put the statements that he has received together with a criminal complaint and seal them so that the Trial Chamber will never be in a position to see them. The same applies to the preliminary interviews conducted both by the police or the investigating judge in case that the -- the witnesses, the privileged witnesses, had decided to change their mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's -- let us just clarify a term here, and I ask Mr. Zecevic to intervene in case we need to intervene in the transcript. In our language it is a similar term, but it is significant. There is a significant difference, so I would like to ask you to clarify that. Yesterday you mentioned the -- that the suspicion that a certain individual has committed a criminal offence. Under our law, the suspicion is graded, so there are different levels of suspicion; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The first and mildest degree of suspicion under the law was referred to as "indications." Indications that a crime has been committed.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time in question and under the law on criminal procedure, that was a term that was applied, "indications," and on the basis of that both the police and the prosecutor would take action. Once the prosecutor has established that there is a higher degree of suspicion, in other words, that there are grounds to suspect that a crime has been committed, then he would take steps to conduct an investigation which would then be assessed by the investigating judge, and if the investigating judge established that there are grounds to suspect, then they would issue a decision to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You have answered three questions that I had in mind but didn't put, so let me just wrap up. The criminal proceedings begin with actions taken by the prosecutor, and then the proceedings can follow one of the two ways. They could issue an indictment directly without an investigation if the conclusion is there is sufficient grounds to suspect, or they would submit a request to the investigating judge to conduct an investigation, and the proceedings will begin at the moment when the investigating judge issues a decision to conduct an investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: From that point on, the suspect is now an accused, and he will be in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I wonder to what extent it is necessary to do this, because it seems to me that this is universal, although the precise methods may change from system to system, that in all criminal matters it begins with a complaint made to the police or investigating authorities, and there's a process through which that complaint is examined, investigated and what not, there is an indictment, there's a trial, and if those who have the duty of proving the guilt of the person satisfy the competent court, there's a conviction. And I don't know that we need evidence to be led that there's a difference between the beginning the process and the -- and the end, because it's only at the end when a competent court convicts anyone that a crime has been established. Do we need evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor dealt with this issue, procedure, and for us it is relevant to just clarify, and that was where my next question was leading when I was interrupted. My next question would have been that from that moment on, and the witness may now answer my question, from that moment on, the criminal proceedings would begin and the police are no longer an active participant in the criminal proceeding. That's what I would like to hear and clarify and the witness to confirm for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've explained so far how criminal proceedings were initiated. Perhaps I should stress it again, I believe I mentioned this yesterday, that the police, before a criminal complaint is submitted, would be busy collecting evidence -- collecting information, and that was their main task. The investigation itself was conducted by the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us just then also shed some light on the role of the Prosecutor, and you will agree with me that this is a specific state organ which had the exclusive authority and practically that was his only work, to prosecute perpetrators of criminal offences by conducting criminal proceeding -- proceedings.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he would do that by -- either by issuing directly an indictment or by issuing a request for initiating criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: He had a special discretionary right where no one could interfere, and that was to decide whether -- whether they would prosecute a perpetrator and to decide also on how the crime would be qualified or described. Is that correct? That was something that the prosecutor decided on exclusively; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And as an investigating judge, you, too, were involved in describing the criminal offence; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Neither you nor the police could affect the decision of the prosecutor on how a criminal offence will be described; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in closing, just a few words about the prosecutor, at any stage of criminal proceedings the prosecutor may suspend proceedings either during the proceedings themselves or -- and even at the late stage immediately preceding the closing, the final resolution of the criminal proceedings; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will now abide by what the Judge has said. We shouldn't deal with legal theory here, and I will just try to go over some of the practical matters that were explored yesterday with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For now, Your Honours, could we have before us P322, Exhibit P322. Can we just have the English version as well. Here we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I believe you were shown this criminal complaint yesterday. This is a criminal report against a group referred to as Zuti Ose, Yellow Wasps; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to page 3 immediately in B/C/S. Here we have it. Can we just zoom in on the first paragraph. Can we also have the English version, please. I'm just waiting for the English version to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please look at the portion where we have the description of a criminal act as provided by the police. In other words, the police believe that in the actions of this group there were elements that pointed to the -- them having committed the criminal offence of aggravated theft; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They say that they have committed a criminal offence from Article 151, which covers serious cases of aggravated theft, robbery, and armed robbery.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The reason I broached this subject is this: I have before me the Criminal Code. I will not refer to it, or I will not open it, but you will trust me when I read out a portion of it. For that particular criminal offence, the sentence that was prescribed was at least five years of prison. At that time the maximum penalty was 15 years. So for this criminal offence the prescribed sentence was 5 to 15 years. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it, and I know that this criminal offence actually consisted a -- a description of the offence which was the aggravated version of the offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just owe it to the Trial Chamber to say that I've referred to the Criminal Code, which is on 65 ter list 3436.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In other words, the police described these actions in such a way that in -- in case that were the case, the sentence of -- or the judgement of arrest would be absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have to say in this case it would not be mandatory, but it would be easier to extend it if necessary based on the information provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. You're correct. One of the elements of this description of -- and prescription of the judgement was that it can -- that this can actually be punishable by a sentence of up to ten years in prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, the prosecutor did not accept this description of the criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter 2487, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We see here a request to conduct an investigation sent to you by the prosecutor. We have to move to page 2 to see the description of the crime chosen by the prosecutor. The penultimate paragraph we can see the description or the qualification of that crime as aggravated theft, Article 148, para 3 of the Criminal Code; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The prescribed sentence for such a crime was up to ten years in prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking off the top of my head, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And detention was not mandatory, i.e., the situation had to be viewed within the broader context, and you as the investigating judge were -- were entitled to release the suspects from detention as soon as such reasons ceased to exist, for them to be kept any longer.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you have explained that yesterday. You did so, because according to the law, detention could only last up to one month, after which it could only be prolonged up to two months if a higher instance court decided so, and if the Supreme Court made a decision to that effect then detention could be extended to up to six months.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor abided by this type of qualification in the indictment stage. It is an exhibit, P317, item 19. These people were charged with aggravated theft rather than robbery, robbery being the more serious crime. My question, hence, is whether you can recall that being the actual indictment.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to see that yesterday on the screen. However, I had not seen that before. I could read that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe we rounded off of this topic. My intention was to illustrate that it was a discretionary right of the prosecutor to provide descriptions or qualifications of the crime and that in that regard he or she was completely independent and no one could influence their work in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Cvijetic, you have mind your point, and you have of covered this area, so there be no reason to venture any further into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Simultaneously with this procedure concerning this type of crime which fell under the category of general crime, one of the group members was also charged with a war crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, those proceedings were handled by the military judiciary, and you said that there were two criteria to decide upon the jurisdiction of that court. One was the status of the perpetrator, i.e., if they were military personnel, and two, the type of crime, if it was indeed a war crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to explain that yesterday. In the first criminal report it was explained in a single paragraph when it said that the accused was handed over to the military prosecutor's office and to the military court in Bijeljina. As we could see, he was interviewed by a military policeman during his detention in the military court about the circumstances of such war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will show you 1D75, which is a Defence exhibit. I suppose you have not had occasion to see this document before, but you can see now that this is an information sheet of the Ministry of the Interior about the particular activity carried out by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the last page so that we could see the very last paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read out the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean that I should do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was able to read was that there was some information held by the Serb armed forces military police, as well as some other authorities of Republika Srpska, to the effect that this person, Dusan Vuckovic, committed a number of crimes, including massacre over the citizens of Muslim ethnicity who were also citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was aware of this at the time, and this is how the prosecutor explained why this person was not included in his request to conduct an investigation. By that time he had been handed over to the military court because he was charged with the war crimes mentioned. Other than that, I cannot explain whether he was later on released from detention or perhaps sent to the court in Sabac -- Samac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Sabac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a fact though that there were proceedings before the court in Sabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to corroborate what you said already, because it says here that he was taken over by the military police. As for Sabac, we have to inform the Judges that this town is not in Bosnia-Herzegovina but in the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia proper; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This Dusan Vuckovic was also a citizen of Serbia, and I presume that was the reason why the case was handed over to their authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You have already answered my next question. You said that you even assisted the competent authorities of Sabac in order to conclude the case. A judgement was finally issued, which is 65 ter number 294.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, where are we going with all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was about to conclude this topic with the witness about the division of jurisdiction between civilian and military prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, this area was covered in extenso yesterday by the Prosecution, and I really don't think that you have added anything new during your cross-examination to this aspect. May I remind the parties that the parties are not at liberty to use as much time as they -- as they would like to but, rather, that they are required to stay focused on the charges raised in the indictment at all times and to stay focused on the issues that were raised during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this topic was covered in examination-in-chief. I don't think this is the right document that we have on the screen, though, but perhaps it is no longer necessary for it to be shown to the witness, because she had not seen it before. I believe this concludes this topic, and I'm ready to move on to the next.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can add something. I was shown the judgement by the Prosecutor during proofing. I was shown the judgement. I think it was by a court in Sabac, and I do remember having contacted them in order to forward the material I had. I also referred them to the military prosecutor's office and the military court to try and obtain the relevant information there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I actually wanted to recall was 65 ter 1294, although I won't be showing it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, since you were investigating judge back in 1992, you also attended on-site investigations, especially in cases of serious crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, therefore, that in 1992 in the territory of Bijeljina municipality, to a large extent, there was an increase of all types of crime and especially serious crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There was an increase in the number of murders as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The number of murders increase significantly. There were exceptionally many murders in the area of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This Chamber is seized of a number of cases of murder which took place within the inter-ethnic context, i.e., in which the perpetrator and the victim were of different ethnicities. There were such murders in Bijeljina as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you discussed with the Prosecutor some of the cases where the victims were Muslims. I wanted to conclude that topic by putting a small number of documents to see -- to see what the outcome of all those cases was. I won't ask you for the exact percentage, but perhaps you can tell us generally what was the ratio between the murders in which victims were Serbs as opposed to the number of murders in which the victims were non-Serbs? Could you share that with us?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak in percentages. It would be far too difficult, and I have never specifically dealt with it. At the time, there was a lot of weapons in Bijeljina. Many murders took place, and I attended many an on-site investigation. Even those I never attended I knew in those cases as well who the victims were, because my colleagues would inform me. In any case, there were more Serb victims than non-Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were there such murders in which there were Serbian victims, whereas the perpetrators were not Serbs? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was in 1992 or 1993, but there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: One of the first murders to take place in which the victim [Realtime transcript read in error "cripple"] was a Muslim was the murder of Salko Kukic of Bijeljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You attended the on-site investigation along side the prosecutor and the civilian police; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend the on-site investigation. It was done by my colleague, Veselin Bozovic, however, I was familiar with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a log-book of the lower prosecutor's office in Bijeljina where we see an entry of a criminal report submitted against the perpetrators of that crime. However, you said that immediately following that the case was referred to the military judiciary for further processing; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have, unless it's already time for the break, to have that criminal report on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You have another six minutes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 1D105.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, you can see here that the public security station in Bijeljina, or the centre of public security, identified the perpetrators initially submitting this criminal report to the basic prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. This is what we can gather from the document.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that. After the on-site investigation and after evidence was collected, the police gathered all relevant information and arrived at the conclusions that these were the persons involved in the murder. They were quick to discover the perpetrators and to submit the criminal report to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move on to the next document immediately. I think it is 65 ter 1286. 1286.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can see here that indeed the military prosecutor took over this case and the proceedings therein by having submitted a request for an investigation. You will agree, since you were familiar with the case, that the threshold was met for this case to be deferred to the military court because these were military conscripts; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were military policemen, and it was known precisely what unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Cvijetic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D00343, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I have -- I seem to have a problem with the previous document and what is said in the transcript about that. You asked the witness: "Were there such murders in which there were Serbian victims, whereas the perpetrators were not Serbs. Can you recall that?" The witness answers: "Yes, there was one. I don't know, in 1992 or 1993." And then you ask one of the first murders to take place in which the -- and there is an odd word in the transcript. What did you mean, the perpetrator or the victim was a Muslim? You asked the witness one of the first murders was to take place in which the "cripple" was a Muslim, was the murder of Salko Kukic, in Bijeljina; correct? So my question is what should -- what did you mean, whether the perpetrators was a Muslim or the victim was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The victim was a Muslim, and that was one of the first murders -- my colleague is telling me that the transcript is wrong about that. The word should be "victim." It seems to have been recorded improperly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then I agree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zecevic is telling me what the word in the transcript was, and now I understand your confusion. Your Honour, I wanted to show the witness another document, but I believe it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we take the break now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have on our screens 65 ter document 2757.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, I think you were shown this document yesterday by the Prosecution, and I think it has been admitted as Exhibit P1541. I just want to follow the chronology as to the outcome of this murder of Salko Kukic. We can see here that after this was deferred to the military court, the prosecutor decided to discontinue prosecution, which resulted in the abandonment of investigation by the investigating judge. Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So whatever we said in introduction with regard the discretionary right of the prosecution is shown here. He exercised this right in order to discontinue the investigation, although he had the perpetrators. He had the qualification of the crime, because there was no doubt that this was a pure criminal murder that was accompanied by robbery. You have seen that.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, because I saw also the on-site investigation report in which this was stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, this was not discussed yesterday, that is to say that in view of the prosecutors abandoning the investigation, since we both worked for the prosecution in the past, we would like to see what was the reason for this decision. You know that the crown witness and the only eyewitness of this murder of Salko Kukic was his wife who was there at the flat when the murder took place. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, after this case, and you should know that as well, she left Republika Srpska, and I think that she's currently living in the federation, or maybe abroad. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no information about that, but I suppose that there must have been a reason for the prosecutor to abandon the proceedings at this particular stage despite the fact that the case was relatively clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If a prosecutor abandons the proceedings at this stage, the investigation can always be resumed once there are conditions met, that is to say when the crown witness or the eyewitness is available to the prosecution organs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Had the prosecutor persisted in issuing an indictment, he would have run a risk of having the accused acquitted due to the lack of evidence because he would miss the crucial piece of evidence, that is to say the eyewitness to the crime. I am speaking theoretically only.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that I don't know what the reasons belie this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you are stating the obvious, and there is no reason to go further here in this matter. You have added nothing new to what was said yesterday, and you have been unable to explain to the witness just -- to the Chamber, sorry, just what exactly turns on the facts that the prosecutor is independent and has a discretion to abandon investigations. So I suggest you move on to something else immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to wrap this up, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these proceedings were continued after the war and if the perpetrators were convicted?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know exactly that after a certain period of time and after the military court stopped working and probably after evidence was obtained, the proceedings were resumed and the perpetrators mentioned in the criminal report submitted by the interior and based on the request from the military court submitted to the military court investigating judge I know that a final judgement was reached, and I know that all these individuals were convicted and are currently either serving the sentence or have already served it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now move to the next case. In your discussion with the Prosecution, and we can see that from your statement as well, you mentioned another extremely serious case in which a family numbering several individuals was killed. That was a Muslim family who was killed in 1992. This family was known in Bijeljina as foster family. Did you discuss this case with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became interested in that particular case because that was truly a very touching and moving event since that was a family of reputable people, and I know that the police worked hard on trying to identify the perpetrators, that they carried out various information-gathering procedures, and I know that the proceedings were instigated before the military court, because the perpetrators were identified, the people who killed those three Muslims, but they also killed another three people of Serbian ethnicity, and the perpetrators were members of the military. I know that they were tried and that they were tried by the military court in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I asked you about this because at the time when you discuss this with the Prosecutor that was in 19 -- in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that respect, can we please have Exhibit 1D034632. 1D034632. It's okay now. I don't think that's the correct document. I'm going to repeat again. 1D034632.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So on page 1 we can see that this is a decision on detention for the perpetrator of these specific individuals. You recognise their names?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are these individuals, and I attended both on-site investigations, that is to say when the three Muslims were killed and then when the three Serbs were killed. And I was assisted by the police of the Bijeljina Public Security Station -- or, rather, public security centre in this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's just look at the next page so that we can see what happened and what the prosecutor did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the next page. That's right. I think that you have to move to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, the military prosecutor took charge of this crime and instituted an investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that number 1 a Serb victim, but there is another portion that deals with the Muslim victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. For that purpose we shall have to see the next page in B/C/S and probably the next page in English as well where we can see the names of the family that we spoke about. You can see under item 2 are the names of the family that we have just mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since Mrs. Simeunovic attended an on-site investigation in this case as an investigating judge, she's fully familiar with this. I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There doesn't appear to be any objection. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D00344. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to test your memory, but can you recall that the initial sentence was death penalty, but can you remember anything about what the sentence was, in fact?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were sentenced to death, but since at the time when this conviction was passed the Dayton Accords were already signed, it became disputable whether death penalty could be effected or not. Therefore, I don't know how this all ended and what sentence they served. Probably 20 years as a substitute for death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I can only confirm that what you said at the very end is correct, because I have the same information. Now let's move to the next case. When I asked you about your on-site investigations, I actually wanted to mention the next case in which you participated. Do you know that at the beginning of the war, apart from the rise of crime rate in Bijeljina there also appeared various paramilitary formations, including those that were involved in illegal trafficking of Muslims into the FRY and Serbia? Are you aware of those activities?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that there were such cases, that people were leaving Bijeljina one -- ones were leaving, the others were coming in, but who did that, I don't know. It is a fact, though, that there were a variety of armed groups, and I think that people thought it was safest to stay indoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: One of those groups executed, so to speak, a number of Muslims, and you were also involved in this case. Do you recall that incident? It happened on the Drina, and I believe that you conducted an on-site investigation. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I cannot tell you exactly what year that was, whether it was 1992 or 1993, but it was impossible to forget such a thing. A large number of Muslims were involved in this case who had been taken away from their house in a brutal manner, took -- taken to the River Drina and killed there. After this became known, the police tried to detect the way in which these people went missing. They managed to gather certain information, and they eventually arrested a number of people. I don't know exactly how many, but I know that among the perpetrators there were four or five or even maybe more individuals who were Serbs, and I clearly remember that there was a Muslim woman among the perpetrators as well. After these people were taken away from their homes, they were taken to the Drina where they were executed. We went to the crime scene. The police called me to join them, but we did not manage to find any clues or evidence. However, detention was imposed because there was other evidence available. There was a request for investigation pursuant to a criminal report that had been submitted, and then on the Drina we tried to reconstruct the event. The police even filmed this area and these proceedings, and that helped us to find certain clues such as bullet casings and other pieces of evidence I can't remember at the moment. But anyway, this helped in providing evidence which ultimately led to the conviction of these perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Simeunovic, some of those murders that took place in 1992 were brought to court either when the perpetrators were apprehended or after evidence was collected at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After an on-site investigation, evidence is collected, but the identity of the perpetrators remained unknown, which prompted the police to continue their work towards detecting the identity of the perpetrators. As far as I know, it seldom happened that such murders remained unsolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecutor showed you the criminal log-book of the basic prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. Can you just confirm that the court as well kept their log-book which showed the phases of criminal proceedings of the cases that we are interested in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: These log-books were also kept by the military prosecutor's office and the military court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This kind of log-book was kept by the police as well. As an investigating judge, you should know about that.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Each police document had its own number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All these organs, and you should know that as well, compiled periodical reports on their work in which they presented statistical data relating to the trends of crime, the successful detection and prosecution of crimes; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me, wouldn't you, that if we want to have a true picture about the number of crime, the percentage of detected crimes that ended in trials, and particularly the crimes that contained this inter-ethnic element, can only be gained after we have gathered all these elements that we spoke about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but to add on that, I would like to add that the court also kept its special log for ongoing investigations, and there was a separate log-book for trials. There was another log-book kept of specific investigating measures such as on-site investigations. They were recorded in a separate log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, in your work -- or, rather, in the work of the Prosecutor's office and the police, did you ever notice different approaches in detecting and prosecuting the perpetrators depending on whether the victims were Muslims or the Serbs? Did you trace any indication of discriminatory approach in their operation?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure that there was no discrimination against any of the victims. I am sure that the police and I, myself, worked diligently in all cases and applied equal approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam, can I just follow up on this answer, because you told the Court either earlier this day or maybe yesterday, I can't remember, you also told the Court that there were more cases involving Serbs as victims than there were cases in which the Muslims were victims. So is your testimony that the -- this difference can be explained only by the fact that more crimes were committed against Serbs than crimes committed against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed murders specifically, and I think we discussed this for the entire war period. Now, I did not make any calculations, nor did anyone show me any statistics, but as far as I know and based on those on-site investigations that I attended, and I attended many, there were far more victims among Serbs and perpetrators among Serbs than the case was with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So maybe I misunderstood your answer earlier on, because I thought you told us that there were more cases in which -- hold on a minute. So your testimony is that the reason why that there were more cases in which Serbs were victims was a reflection of the facts, namely that more crimes were committed against Serbs. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can explain it in the following manner: The majority of the population in Bijeljina was Serb, and that was the reason why there was a greater percentage, and we don't know exactly what that percentage is, but I know from my work that the number of Serb victims was greater than the number of murdered Muslims at that time in that period between 1992 and 1995, because I attended most of those on-site investigations, and the explanation for me of that is that the majority of the population was Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And therefore your conclusion is that because -- or since the majority of the population was Serb, it was only natural that the majority of crimes were also committed against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, the last thing that is left to be clarified is to look into the motives for some of these gravest criminal offences. Would you agree with my conclusion that all of these murders were purely criminal murders, the classic type of murder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, is that a proper question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will rephrase my question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, do you know what the predominant motive was in the perpetration of these most serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Isn't that the same question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I put a direct question now. I did not put a leading question. I was asking the witness whether she knew what was the motive behind these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but her role as an investigating judge, she, as a matter of common sense, may have deduced some motive. It's speculative. It's her conclusion, this matter of any assistance to the Tribunal. It's really neither here nor there. She's entitled to draw a personal conclusion, but it's really irrelevant, isn't it? She is entitled to draw conclusions. So are you. So is everybody else observing the facts that with which we are concerned but those conclusions are not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will rephrase yet again my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What -- can you tell us, all of these accused, what crimes were they charged with?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the crime of murder as described in Article 36 and perhaps 37. I can't tell you the exact paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move on, Ms. Simeunovic, to one other question. You had occasion to co-operate with the police in the course of your work, so you should be familiar with the hierarchy within the police, so let me ask you this: In 1992, how well were you acquainted with the chain of command, as it were, the hierarchy within the police?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not really go into this, nor did I pay much attention to the police hierarchy. That was not something that was the focus of my work. I -- for the most part I had contacts with inspectors and forensic technicians. I never had occasion to attend any kind of meeting or gathering with the chiefs of police or whatever their titles were, but I do know that in 1992 there were frequent changes, personnel changes, within the police. And at that time, in early 1992, when the whole thing began, when the police was established I can't really tell you what it was called, but it was in SAO Semberija and Majevica originally, and then later on that name changed, but I can't tell you exactly what the name of the police organ was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So in those early days it was established at the level of the municipality and at the regional level, which is the SAO Semberija and Majevica, or the Serbian autonomous districts; correct? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, up until those events from early 1992, Bijeljina was a municipality and it had a police force at that level. The higher level was, as far as I know from my work -- oh, both for -- this refers both to the police and the judicial organs. The higher level was in Tuzla. However, in 1992, Bijeljina's jurisdiction was extended to surrounding places such as Lopari and similar, so that this was the area that I was familiar with, and I know the people who were in charge of those areas and who operated there. In other words, in Bijeljina, Ugljevik, in other words, within the Bijeljina municipality and on its outskirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, did you know who the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would now like to show you an "Official Gazette," that's what it was called, of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pull up 65 ter 2442, under tab -- the Prosecutor's tab 62. Very well. Could we please pull up page 8 in the B/C/S version, and in English that would be page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version on this page, the last paragraph we see an article.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just zoom in on the bottom part of the page where we see 230. That's in the right column, right-hand column, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here we just see who passed this decision, and now I would just like to move on to the next page in the B/C/S version, because we don't really see much on this page, that's page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us now zoom in. Let's look at the upper left-hand corner. Let's zoom in on that and see the decision. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, please take a look briefly at this decision in the English version. We have the relevant first two articles. We probably don't need the others.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, we see here that this decision of the Presidency envisages that women, too, will be conscripts in the conditions in which the Serbian Republic found itself. Do you agree with me? Is that what we can infer from this?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking this is the following: Were you assigned -- were you assigned any duties? Did you get any kind of schedule?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive a decision or a written decision, I can't recall exactly, on my wartime assignment, and I, Biljana Simeunovic; and it said "Conscript - is hereby assigned to work duty as a judge," and this came from the military office in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now if we can look at page 15 of this same "Official Gazette" in the B/C/S version and 18 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, I suppose that you can recognise your first and last name, so in this "Official Gazette," your appointment as judge was actually punished; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I observed looking back, page by page, in this same "Official Gazette" that some 19 or so people were assigned to various judicial posts; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the correct figure, together with the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And I think that I came across some six names that were non-Serb. So is that correct? Do you -- can you confirm that there were also non-Serb colleagues who were elected or appointed at that time as judges?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know, although I was absent at the time from the area, but I do know, for instance, that Mr. Alija Zvizdic, specifically, I know of his case, that he was elected at this time. And to this day, he is the president of the lower court in Bijeljina. He was elected as judge at the same time when I was. I know. I recall that clearly. There were some others, but I can't really recall. We can see it if we look at this "Official Gazette."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please just see the previous page in both versions, just to see a few sample names. In the B/C/S also, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here you can see that there is a colleague of yours, a woman, a Ms. Alma Salihbegovic also elected; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under number 263.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If we go one page back again.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under number 255 we can see Alija Zvizdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you can also see above that Alida Nad-Madzarac [phoen] another name.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now let's go back another page. Here you can see the names of Vinko Vusadin and Muhamed Gluhonic as well as Ismail Salihbegovic.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we were all elected at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please just tell us what nationality were these people?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Vinka Vusadin was Croat. Ismail Salihbegovic has got to be Muslim. Muhamed Gluhonic is Muslim. I mean now we would use the term Bosniaks, but at that time we used the word Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. Simeunovic, thank you very much. I have completed my cross-examination, and I have no further questions for you. Thank you for testifying before this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Simeunovic. I do not have many questions for you, because this municipality was not mentioned in the indictment against my client, Mr. Zupljanin, so I will be brief. In answering the questions from the Prosecutor regarding the competences of the military prosecutor and military courts, you told us what you knew about that situation. In order to assist this Trial Chamber, could you please describe what the context was at the time that is the subject of this indictment, 1992, which was a time of war? So you mentioned already that the court was in the process of being established on all the other government agencies, so the entire situation was confusing and rather grim in view of the fact that it was wartime; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the course of your regular duties, I suppose that you encountered a number of difficulties such as some very basic work conditions. For instance, office supplies, technical aspects and so on. Very frequently, for instance, there were power blackouts. So could you describe the conditions in which you worked in 1992, briefly.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that we worked in very difficult conditions. There were periods with power cuts lasting up to one or two months in continuum. And when there was electricity, it came on every three or four days for some eight hours a day. Therefore, I wouldn't even be able to tell you any longer whether we had a telefax or photocopiers at our disposal. Even if we did, we had no electricity to use them. And I'm certain that in the court building where I worked there was no heating. The on-site investigations we also conducted had to be done under difficult circumstances. Frequently we did not even have torch lights if this happened at night-time, and then we used car lights, and there were very few cars at the time. Sometimes six or seven or eight of us would attend a scene of crime in a single vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your last sentence was not entered into the transcript. I think you said you and your colleagues, given the shortage of vehicles when attending scenes of crimes, often went together and some of you even had to sit back in the trunk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I also omitted to say that even the phone lines were down. It was very difficult to get in touch with an investigating judge. The police frequently had to come and fetch me from my village, and they would find me working in my garden.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In such wartime circumstances, as is generally known here, practically all police forces were mobilised and resubordinated to military units, because in particular in the region of Bijeljina, there were many combat operations which took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know that. I really would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we have this specific situation as you have said in one of the answers to Mr. Olmsted's questions yesterday concerning the competencies of the military judiciary: When there was a crime against civilians in a combat area, then in terms of jurisdiction an on-site investigation should be carried out by a member of the military judiciary, that is to say a military prosecutor or a military investigative judge and the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Any person, irrespective of their position, if they have information about a crime, is obliged to report the crime to the competent authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Hence in a situation in which, let's say -- well, I'm not saying this is true, but if you have such information, do share it with us. If someone reports that specifically non-Serbs were killed in a village, and if at that moment if there was a police patrol or police organs nearby, they would carry out initial measures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is also foreseen by the law on criminal procedure in cases where the competent court was not the lower court but a higher court, or if there was no territorial jurisdiction, then such a court would be tasked with carrying out initial activities and then to refer it to the competent court. If there were urgent investigative measures to be undertaken irrespective of subject matter and territorial jurisdiction, they simply had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is also missing from the transcript. You mentioned securing evidence and securing the scene of crime in order to preserve as much evidence as possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then, of course, any further procedures transferred to the military investigative authorities which would then carry out their own on-site investigation and so on.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are still following the line you began with your initial question in cases where there were crimes against civilians, and in case these were war crimes, then the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I was trying to draw a clear distinction, and perhaps you can tell the Chamber something that is based on your own experience, there were a great many murders in Bijeljina in the town itself, in the urban part where there had not been combat, and of course in such circumstances the competent authorities were the civilian authorities and judiciary, and in that case they were in charge of the whole procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We don't have your answer recorded. Could you please repeat it. Yes. It's in there now. The greatest problem is in understanding the competencies of the police in such a situation. Say -- you are now a prosecutor with the federal prosecutor's office. In 1991 [as interpreted], amidst a war chaos, it was very difficult to get by witness statements and solid evidence in terms of potential war crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
